meters.label: Missing-id lookups at the database per second

frames.narration: Normal minute. The top-deals entry sits in the cache with a 60 second TTL. All 1,000 requests per second are hits, and the database only sees the 100 queries per second from the rest of the site.
At 60 seconds the TTL runs out and the entry disappears. Nothing is wrong yet: the next request will find an empty slot.

The stampede. The rebuild takes 2 seconds, so every request that arrives in that time misses, and each one asks the database for the same answer. That is about 1,000 identical queries in the first second, on top of the 100 already running.

The database can serve about 500 queries per second, so it slows down. The rebuild now takes longer than 2 seconds, so even more requests arrive before the entry is back, and the pile grows. Retrying clients make it worse.

Fix 1: request coalescing. At the next expiry the first request starts the rebuild and the app records "top-deals is loading". The other 999 requests wait for that answer. The database gets 1 query, so it is back to 101 per second.

Fix 2: refresh early. At 54 seconds, 90% of the TTL, one background task rebuilds the entry while the old copy is still served. Requests normally never see a miss. TTL jitter of plus or minus 10% also keeps different entries from expiring in the same second.

states.cache: old copy served until new one lands

frames.narration: A different leak. Bots repeat 300 requests per second for 50 product ids that do not exist. There is nothing to store, so each lookup misses and goes to the database, which answers "not found". The database now carries 401 queries per second.

Negative caching: the app stores a "not found" marker for each missing id with a 30 second TTL. Each of the 50 ids is now looked up once per 30 seconds, about 2 queries per second, and the database is down to 103.

Now a seller changes a price. Write-through updates the database and the cache before replying: slower, but reads are fresh and nothing is lost. Write-back would reply after writing only the cache and flush later, which is faster but loses the change if the cache node dies first. Write-around would write only the database and let the next read refill the cache.
